text.p: President Bill Clinton, denying he is a "closet liberal," said on Monday the crushing Republican landslide in the 1994 elections had a sobering impact on fellow Democrats, who now back a moderate agenda.

Clinton insisted he was ignoring polls giving him a huge lead over Republican rival Bob Dole and Reform Party nominee Ross Perot, saying the "weight of history" has been against incumbent Democrats. Only two Democrats in the last century have won re-election.

In a television interview, Clinton brushed aside the latest political strategy by Dole -- designed to portray the president as a liberal who is trying to mask his true feelings until after the Nov. 5 election.

"I know its convenient for the Republicans to raise the flag of oh, these people would be so liberal if you let them. Clinton will be liberal in his second term," the president said in an interview with "The NewsHour with Jim Lehrer."
"The problem with that argument, it doesn't fit with what I did as president ... and won't fit with what I'm planning to do in my second term," Clinton said.
He said that Democrats had learned from the 1994 debacle in which Republican gained control of both houses of Congress for the first time in four decades.
"I think the Democratic Party was sobered by what happened in the ... '94 elections, and I believe we have a high degree of focus on the future," Clinton said.
Earlier, during an exchange with reporters in the Oval Office, Clinton also challenged the Republican claim he has a liberal agenda.

"The record doesn't support the charge," Clinton said, citing several programmes and policies that he said had a decidedly non-liberal cast -- including welfare reform, tough anti-crime measures and deficit reduction.

"It is true that (Dole) and I had differences over the budget last year and we will again in this campaign. And we have different tax cut plans. But I don't think that qualifies me as a closet liberal," Clinton said.
With tongue in cheek, he added: "the president is too exposed. I don't have a closet."

While the Democratic president made light of Dole's effort to brand him a liberal -- now considered by many a dirty word in the lexicon of American politics -- his spokesman accused the Republican candidate of taking the low road.

Dole and his supporters "utterly ... have gone negative and that is a source of concern because it degrades prospects for a vigorous debate about the two different visions for the future that are out there -- the president's versus Mr. Dole's," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.

In his television interview, Clinton downplayed the wide lead he holds in opinion polls. "I don't take that entirely seriously. I think that we have to run as if we're dead even, a little behind. We have to remember the weight of history is against us."
"It's been a long time since a Democrat has been re-elected," he said. Franklin Roosevelt was the last Democratic re-elected as president.
He also spoke fondly of Dick Morris, his political strategist who was forced to resign following an uproar over a report he was involved with a prostitute for some two years.
"He worked hard for me, he did the best he could," Clinton said of Morris, who was credited with having had a major role in the president's political revival.
Clinton said Morris is "a very gifted man. He's a very brilliant man" and that he hoped the political stategist and his wife, Eileen McGann, "can put their lives together and go on."
